opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it shifted my view somewhat, though maybe not in the direction people might expect.

When the constitutional AI work came out, the striking thing was that you could write down a set of fairly abstract principles in natural language, like "choose the response that is least harmful" or "avoid being preachy," and the model could use them to critique and revise its own outputs in a way that actually tracked what those principles meant, at least most of the time. That's not trivial. It suggests these models have absorbed a lot of the structure of how humans talk and argue about norms. They can tell when a principle applies, notice tensions between principles, and produce something that looks like a justification.

So in one sense it updated me toward thinking language models have real competence in normative reasoning, or at least a very good model of normative discourse.

But I also came away more convinced that this isn't the same thing as the kind of normative reasoning we ultimately want from AI systems. A few reasons.

First, the principles in a constitution are underspecified. "Be helpful, harmless, and honest" doesn't settle what to do in hard cases. What fills the gap is the model's learned prior over how people would interpret those words, and that prior is opaque. We don't really know which conception of harm or helpfulness it's using, or whether it's consistent across contexts.

Second, my own work has argued that alignment shouldn't be framed as aligning to one set of preferences or one fixed list of values. Human normativity is much more about roles, social practices, and agreements between people who disagree. What a good assistant should do depends on who it's serving, in what role, and under what norms that role carries. A single constitution, however well written, flattens that. It's closer to one authority's specification than to something people with different values could reasonably agree to.

Third, there's a gap between producing good normative text and reasoning in a way that's reliable and inspectable. When a model revises an answer according to a principle, I want to know: did it actually infer what the principle requires, or did it pattern-match to what a revised answer usually looks like? Those come apart in exactly the novel, high-stakes cases we care about most.

So my overall take is that constitutional AI showed language models are a surprisingly useful substrate for representing norms and applying them flexibly. That's genuinely valuable, and I think it's part of the toolkit going forward. But it also made clearer to me that we need more structure around it: explicit representations of whose norms apply and why, ways for different stakeholders to contest and negotiate those norms, and inference methods that let us check that the system is reasoning about the principles rather than just imitating what that reasoning sounds like.

r001.rationale: The response says models can critique and revise their outputs using abstract principles in ways that track the principles’ meaning, and treats this as evidence that they have absorbed normative structure. This conveys implicit learning of how to apply such principles.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I should say up front that before constitutional AI, I was fairly skeptical. My background is in Bayesian cognitive science and inverse reinforcement learning, and the whole frame I'd been working in was that getting values into a system is a hard inference problem. You observe behavior, you infer preferences or norms, and the natural-language description of what you want is at best a noisy hint. So when people started saying "just write down the principles and have the model follow them," my instinct was that this was going to be brittle in exactly the ways rule-based systems have always been brittle. You write "be helpful," and the model either over-applies it or under-applies it, because the rule doesn't carry its own conditions of application with it.

What surprised me about constitutional AI was less the alignment result and more what it revealed about the models. The fact that you could hand a model a principle like "choose the response that is less likely to be harmful or manipulative," have it critique its own output against that principle, and get something that looked like reasonable application in novel cases, that told me the model already had a lot of implicit knowledge about what those words mean in context. It wasn't learning the norm from scratch; it was being pointed at a norm it had largely absorbed from human text. And that actually fit with a view I'd been developing, that a lot of what we call normative reasoning in humans is also not derivation from axioms. It's a kind of flexible pattern-matching over a huge store of cases, plus the ability to articulate reasons when asked.

So it shifted me in two directions at once. On one hand, I updated toward thinking that language models can do a meaningful amount of the work of interpreting principles, of filling in the context-dependent part that I'd assumed would need to be learned from behavior. On the other hand, it made me more cautious about calling that "reasoning about normative principles" in the strong sense. Because the thing that makes a constitution work in a human society isn't just that individuals can read it. It's that there are institutions, contestation, precedent, people who disagree and have to justify themselves to each other. A model self-critiquing against a fixed list of principles is doing a kind of monologue. It can be impressively sensible, and it can also just confabulate a justification for whatever it was going to do anyway, and from the outside those look very similar.

So my current view is something like: constitutional AI showed me that the interpretive bottleneck was smaller than I thought, and the legitimacy and verification bottlenecks are bigger than people tend to acknowledge. The model can tell you what the principle plausibly implies. Whether that's the right implication, and who gets to say so, is still an open question that no amount of self-critique inside one model is going to resolve.

r001.rationale: The response says that a model’s ability to critique its output against a principle and apply it in novel cases showed it already had implicit knowledge of the norm, largely absorbed from human text.

astra-6.text:
Constitutional AI made me take more seriously the possibility that language models could reason with explicitly stated normative principles. You can give a model a principle, ask it to critique a response in light of that principle, and then have it revise the response. That suggests principles can play a functional role in guiding behavior, beyond simply appearing in the text a model produces.

But I’d distinguish that from having a robust understanding of what makes a principle justified, or how to resolve conflicts between principles. A model might produce a convincing critique while applying the same principle inconsistently in another context. So it shifted my assessment toward seeing these models as potentially useful components of systems that reason about norms, while leaving open the harder questions about reliability, justification, and whose norms they should follow.

r001.rationale: The candidate says a model can critique and revise a response using a supplied principle, suggesting principles can guide behavior. It does not say this ability shows the model had already implicitly learned how to comply with those principles.

sol-6.1.text:
Constitutional AI was a pretty significant update for me. Before that, I was more skeptical that language models could take an abstract normative principle and apply it meaningfully to a particular situation. You might get them to repeat a principle, but that’s different from using it to critique an answer and then improve it.

What constitutional AI showed was that you could give a model a set of principles in natural language and have it do some of that work: identify where a response conflicted with a principle, explain the conflict, and revise the response. That suggested there was more capacity for normative reasoning there than I had expected.

I’d distinguish that from having demonstrated that the model reliably understands those principles or will follow them in every new context. But it changed my sense of what was possible. Principles could be more than statements we trained a model to recite; they could actually help guide its behavior.

r001.rationale: The response says models could identify conflicts with supplied principles and revise answers, suggesting more normative reasoning capacity than expected. It does not say this showed they had already implicitly learned how to comply with those principles.
